title: A tilted spinning gyroscope doesn't fall over: it circles sideways instead

cover.alt: A metal gyroscope in a spherical cage, balanced at a tilt on top of a small pedestal.

body: Gravity pulling on a tilted gyroscope creates a twisting force, a torque, that would topple it if it weren't spinning. A spinning wheel responds differently: the torque swings its axis sideways, at right angles to the push, so the tilted axis traces out a cone instead of falling. This is **gyroscopic precession**, the same motion as a wobbling spinning top. The faster the spin, the slower the circling: the precession rate is the torque divided by the wheel's spin angular momentum, so a top that is slowing down circles faster and faster.

slides.alt: A gyroscope in a metal cage sits tilted on the tip of a pedestal. It doesn't fall; instead the whole tilted gyroscope keeps swinging round in a circle.
slides.caption: Spun up by a motor and balanced at a tilt on a pedestal, the gyroscope doesn't topple. Its tilted axis keeps swinging round in a circle instead.

slides.question: Earth precesses too, like a giant top. How many years does its axis take to trace one full circle?
slides.explanation: About 26,000 years. The Sun and Moon pull on Earth's bulging equator, trying to drag it into line with our orbit; instead, the torque makes the axis precess.

slides.heading: Where precession shows up
items: Earth's axis, which drifts away from Polaris

slides.question: As a gyroscope's spin slows down, what happens to its circling?
slides.explanation: The precession rate is the torque divided by the wheel's spin angular momentum, so less spin means faster circling.
